name: Elihu
interpretive_note: Elihu's role is debated: some readers treat his speeches as a needed corrective bridge to God's own answer, since God's later rebuke (Job 38:1-40:2) is directed only at Job and the three friends, not at Elihu by name; others read Elihu as another voice of human wisdom that, however closer to the truth, still falls short of God's own answer out of the whirlwind. Job itself does not explicitly evaluate Elihu's speeches as right or wrong.
source_summary: A younger man, angry at both Job and his three friends, who speaks at length in Job 32-37, defending God's justice and greatness before God Himself finally answers Job out of the whirlwind.
family_friendly_summary: Elihu was a young man who had been listening quietly while Job and his three older friends argued about why Job was suffering so much. Elihu grew frustrated -- with Job, for defending himself instead of trusting God, and with the three friends, for failing to really answer Job's hard questions. So Elihu spoke up, even though he was younger than everyone else there. He gave several long speeches reminding everyone how great and just God is, and that God often teaches people through suffering rather than only punishing them for sin. Right after Elihu finished speaking, God Himself began to speak to Job out of a whirlwind.
adult_story: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite is introduced late in the book of Job, after Job's three friends -- Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar -- have exhausted their arguments and fallen silent, unable to answer Job's protests of innocence (Job 32:1). Elihu, who has held back out of respect for his elders, says his anger has burned against Job "because he justified himself before God," and against the three friends because "they had not found an answer, although they had condemned Job" (32:2-3). Across four chapters (32-37) he delivers Job's longest single speech, insisting that God is greater than any human accuser, that God speaks through affliction to turn people from pride, and that God's justice and power in creation should silence Job's demand for an explanation (33:14-30; 36:22-33; 37:14-24). Elihu's tone is confident to the point of self-important -- he repeatedly announces how much he has to say -- yet his emphasis on God's transcendence and use of suffering to instruct rather than merely punish anticipates themes God Himself takes up immediately afterward, speaking to Job out of the whirlwind (38:1). Notably, Elihu is never named among those God rebukes at the book's end (42:7-9), unlike the three friends, though Scripture does not explicitly commend him either -- his exact place in the book's argument remains genuinely debated.
christ_connections: Elihu's insistence that God may use suffering not as punishment but as instruction points toward the New Testament's fuller revelation that suffering can produce endurance and Christlike character in those who belong to God (Romans 5:3-5; Hebrews 12:5-11).

Elihu longs for a mediator who could arbitrate between God and Job (Job 33:23-24, "a mediator... to tell a man what is right for him") -- a role Job himself later says he lacks (9:33) and which the New Testament identifies as fulfilled in Christ, "the one mediator between God and mankind" (1 Timothy 2:5).
devotionals: Elihu’s story teaches us about God's justice; may we look to Jesus, whose grace and truth never fail.
Through Elihu’s experience of suffering, God teaches us to trust His wisdom and follow Jesus faithfully.
